That new green nub on your moth orchid could be a flower spike. They tend to show up in November, and the right care this month gives them the best chance.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Sometime in early November, a moth orchid (Phalaenopsis) on the windowsill might push out new growth. It could be a root, but it could also be the start of a flower spike – and that's why orchids in November deserve a closer look than they got all summer.

All of this happens right as basic orchid care gets harder, too. The days are shorter, and less light gets through the glass. The furnace has kicked on by now, drying out the indoor air, and the bark in the pot stays wet much longer than it did in July. Roots left sitting wet can go soft. Buds sometimes yellow and drop off before they open.

Thankfully, you don't need to do anything dramatic. Most of it is moving a pot a little closer to the window, feeling the bark before you water, or shifting the plant out of a draft. Changes made now, while spikes are just getting started, give a moth orchid a better shot at a full display later in winter or into spring.

Cooler fall temperatures are the main trigger for flower spikes in moth orchids, and shorter days may help a little, so this is the month when plenty of growers start spotting them. The trouble is, spikes and aerial orchid roots look a lot alike when they first poke out. Look closely at the tip, and you can usually tell. Roots come to a bit of a point. Back from the tip, they're wrapped in a spongy layer that goes silvery when it's dry and turns green after you water. Spikes don't have that coating at all. They're green the whole way up, and the end is rounded and closed off, kind of like a mitten.

Before attempting to train a new orchid flower spike, give it some time to grow on its own first. When it's several inches long, push a stake into the bark close to the base. Angle it a little so you don't spear a root. Then clip the spike to it loosely, adding another clip higher up every so often as it grows. Orchid flowers don't always grow completely straight, so you may have more success with bendable stakes, like these Sproot stakes with clips on Amazon.

Flowers might still be a couple of months off, or longer, so Christmas blooms on every plant aren't a sure thing. Once buds show, quit turning the pot around – they'll grow toward whatever light they're getting.

That shady spot that kept a moth orchid from scorching in July can be too dim by November. Low light can keep a mature plant from spiking at all, and it can also cause bud drop later on.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

An east window is a good choice right now to meet your orchid's light requirements. South and west windows work too, as long as a sheer curtain softens the harshest afternoon sun – direct rays can still overheat buds and burn leaves.

Watch the glass, though. On a frosty night, a pane can get cold enough to damage a leaf resting against it, so leave some space between the plant and the window. Not every house has a sunny window open for one more pot, and a grow light can make up for that. This Sansi clip-on grow light clips right onto the pot.

Bark that dried out in no time over the summer can hang onto water much longer in a cool, dim room. Often, orchids get into trouble on a fixed watering schedule this time of year.

So how do you know when it's time to water orchids? Look at the roots. Silvery, whitish roots are dry, and green ones still have water in them. Lift the pot to feel its weight, too, since a light one is another clue

Clear plastic orchid pots, like these from Walmart, make it easier to check. Moisture meters are less reliable with orchids, but some growers like to use a Sustee Aquameter stick for a second opinion. It turns white once the mix dries out.

When it is time to water, give it a real soak. Take the pot to the sink and run room-temperature water through it till it pours out the bottom. Let it drain all the way. If any water is sitting where the leaves meet, tip it out.

Bark tells you more, honestly, than the calendar will. But bone-dry all winter is the wrong move. Moth orchids don't go dormant, and roots that sit dry for weeks can shrivel.

Kept warm around the clock, a moth orchid can go on growing leaves for months without sending up a spike. That seems a little backward, if you think about it, for a tropical plant. Cooler temperatures encourage flower spikes, and nights around 60–65°F (16–18°C) for a few weeks in fall can help. Daytime heat matters too, and a spot by a heat vent that keeps the plant much above 80°F (27°C) for long stretches can hold spiking back.

Cooler doesn't mean cold. Try to keep moth orchids above about 55°F (13°C), and don't park them by an outside door or a leaky window.

After buds form, forget about the temperature drop. Steady conditions matter more at that point. A cold blast every time the door opens can make buds yellow and fall before they open, and so can hot air blowing off a register.

Growth slows down this month, and slower growth uses less fertilizer. How much to cut back depends on the plant and where it's sitting. Under a grow light in a warm room, a moth orchid may still be making new leaves and roots. On a cool windowsill, it might barely grow at all.

Other types of orchids are a different story, and a few kinds need a drier, leaner rest through winter – check the type before you change anything.

Not feeding at all is its own kind of mistake, though, just a quieter one. Moth orchids cut off from fertilizer while spikes form or flowers open can end up with fewer blooms. A diluted dose of an all-purpose orchid fertilizer, mixed as directed on the label, keeps them going. One option is Better-Gro Orchid Plus, available at Walmart, a 20-14-13 formula sold in a 1-pound (454 g) bag.

Bloom boosters aren't the shortcut they sound like. Moth orchids fed a balanced formula will often produce more flowers than those given high-phosphorus fertilizer.

Bud blast is the term growers use when buds turn yellow and fall off before they open. Heating season brings plenty of the usual causes. Dry furnace air is one. So is a radiator sitting too close, or a cold draft every time the door opens. Bark that keeps swinging from soaked to bone dry doesn't help either.

Fruit on the counter is a sneaky one, oddly enough – as it ripens, it gives off ethylene gas that can make buds drop, so keep budded orchids away from the fruit bowl.

Damp pebbles in a tray under the pot raise the humidity a little, like this Brussel's humidity tray with decorative rocks. In a very dry room, a small humidifier, like this compact Pure Enrichment MistAire Studio humidifier, adds moisture without taking up much space.

While you're watering, look the plant over for orchid pests. Mealybugs usually turn up on the spike or where a leaf joins the stem. Something that looks like a bit of white cotton stuck in there is probably the long-tailed mealybug (Pseudococcus longispinus) or citrus mealybug (Planococcus citri). Boisduval scale (Diaspis boisduvalii) looks nothing like that. You'll find it as small, flat bumps on the leaves, almost like they're part of the plant. Both pests weaken an orchid and spread to others nearby.

Wipe off the ones you can see with a cotton swab dipped in rubbing alcohol. If they keep coming back, switch to an insecticidal soap or horticultural oil labeled for orchids. Safer Brand Insect Killing Soap, available at Walmart, is one option that targets mealybugs and other common houseplant pests. Test a small area first, then repeat treatment as directed on the label to catch newly hatched pests.

Routine orchid repotting can wait. It's easier on the plant when fresh roots are actively growing, often after flowering finishes, and root disturbance while a spike develops can set it back. The exception is bark that's broken down into mush or roots that have gone brown and soft – that plant needs fresh mix now, spike or no spike.

Leave healthy green spikes alone, too. One without buds yet may still flower, and there's no sense tossing away blooms you might've had. Cold glass is another one to watch on the coldest nights, so pull the leaves back if they're touching the window. Then there's the crown, where the new leaves come out of the center. Water that sits in there can cause crown rot. If that rot reaches the growing point, the plant has no way of making new leaves from the top again.

Most of what an orchid needs in November is a little attention. Spot the new spike, lift the pot before you water, and notice the draft by the back door. Get those right, and there's a good chance of a long run of flowers sometime between midwinter and spring. That's not bad for moving a pot a few feet.

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. #8037. 19 Great Gift Ideas That Are HSA/FSA Eligible

Bonus: They’re all literally proven to be good for you, too!

Here’s a fun fact about your Flexible Spending Account (FSA): whatever you don’t spend by the deadline is gone. Granted, some plans give you a little grace period or rollover a small amount, but most of us are on the use-it-or-lose-it clock. And while Health Savings Account (HSA) money doesn’t expire, it’s still sitting there earmarked for your health, and the holidays are a good excuse to finally use it.

What’s great is that you can buy a lot more with it than just your basic bandages or the odd bottle of contact solution. We’re talking heating pads, period underwear, sunscreen, smart rings... even ergonomic office chairs can qualify! Some of the bigger-ticket items here (like the Lettuce Grow) may require a letter of medical necessity, but that typically just means filling out a quick online health questionnaire at checkout through a service like Truemed or Flex. Everything else you can usually just swipe your HSA/FSA card for. Of course, rules vary by plan, so check yours if you’re not sure.

One important caveat: HSA/FSA funds can only be used for you, your spouse, and your dependents. That means the following picks are perfect for treating yourself, stuffing your kids’ stockings, or, you know, finally getting your snoring partner something that’ll ultimately help you both sleep.

Here are some of our favorite items that are often covered by HSA and FSA guidelines.

If you know someone who gets painful period cramps or has endometriosis or adenomyosis, these little menstrual heat pads are such a thoughtful stocking stuffer. I stick them inside the waistband of my pants, and it genuinely gets hot enough to offer relief and go wherever I go all day. They last for hours, and I just love that they let me get relief without feeling stuck to a heating pad (and therefore a wall outlet). — Katie McPherson

Isn’t it great when really trendy, great-smelling, cute beauty products are also good for you and eligible to buy with tax-exempt money? This is the case with Touchland hand sanitizer, which is all the rage with tweens and teens, and for good reason. It’s so cute and fun that it makes keeping germs away a blast. This is so perfect for stocking stuffing. — Sarah Aswell

As someone who works from home, I’ve always struggled with back pain from sitting hunched over a laptop all day long. I never even thought to check whether an office chair could be HSA/FSA-eligible... until I found out about Branch, which is usually through Truemed. Yes, you typically need to fill out a short form to get a letter of medical necessity, but it’s so worth it if the end result is a beautiful Branch office chair with 14 points of adjustment, including lumbar support that moves up, down, in and out, with armrests that adjust five ways. It’s also nice that there are so many upholstery options (I ordered the black boucle!). — Julie Sprankles

While not all DNA kits are eligible for HSA and FSA spending accounts, ones that give you health information are usually kosher. This one, from Ancestry, falls into that category. Have fun learning more about yourself and your past while also finding out medical information that could change your life. This is a great gift for someone who has everything. — Sarah Aswell

One of the most popular purchases with FSA and HSA money is this heated massage gun. It feels amazing, and it makes you feel better in the long run. We like this one because it gets killer reviews and comes with an app. Again, this is a big-ticket item that might turn out to be a great way to spend FSA money at the end of the year. — Sarah Aswell

I have a chronic illness that causes high inflammation, so I tend to have a lot of body pain... especially in my joints. This flexible, wearable device combines red light, infrared light, micro-vibration, and micro-magnetic pulses in one band. I’ve found that if I strap it on to whatever aches, it really seems to help ease the pain. You should be able to pay directly with your HSA/FSA card, but it’s always a good idea to check with your specific health plan to see if you need a letter of medical necessity. — Julie Sprankles

Supergoop is one of my favorite beauty products and by far my favorite sunscreen company. They make my skin look and feel great while protecting it for the future. Many of Supergoop’s products are FSA- and HSA-eligible, including this mineral eye cream that works like a dream. But don’t sleep on many of their other products — I also love their Unseen Sunscreen for faces. — Sarah Aswell

I am not exaggerating when I say that my life was changed by breaking down and getting an electric heating pad for my bed. It makes my sore body feel better, it prevents stiffness, and it is also just really, really nice when I have my period and I’m feeling crampy. — Sarah Aswell

This smart scale tracks 16 metrics, including muscle mass, body fat, and heart rate. You can pick the ones you want to show on the big color display and hide the rest, and it recognizes up to eight users. Plus, it syncs up with Apple Health and Google Health. Oh, and it has a few fun extra modes: Baby Mode (in case you need to check before your next pediatrician visit), Pet Mode (if your pup is on a diet), and Luggage Mode (so you know before heading to the airport). — Julie Sprankles

I’m not proud of it, but in my middle age I’ve become a pretty bad snorer. The best gift I’ve ever gotten for my partner is these Ozlo earbuds, which can’t be beat. They are really comfortable to sleep in, and the white noise makes you catch your Zs like a baby. The price is a bit splurgy, but can you put a dollar sign on deep sleep, especially if you can put it on your HSA card? — Sarah Aswell

Man, do some reading about blue light glasses, and you’ll see that they have virtually no downside — especially if you wear them at night while looking at screens. It’s probably the best thing you can buy for yourself under $20 that can help you feel better and get better sleep. And VisoOne has some really cute styles, too. — Sarah Aswell

I’ve always wanted an Oura ring but held off because (a) I’m a mom and tend to buy everything for everyone else first and (b) this is more than I normally spend on myself. So I was pleasantly surprised to find out it’s HSA/FSA-eligible! The Oura Ring 4 looks like regular jewelry but tracks more than 50 metrics like sleep, stress, heart health, cycle, and more, which is hugely helpful always but especially when you’re in perimenopause like so many of us on the Scary Mommy team are. — Julie Sprankles

I love giving first-aid kits to people for the holidays, especially if someone has recently gotten a new car, moved into a new place, or had a new baby. Saalt Hanky Panky Boy Short Period Underwear

My favorite pair is these boy shorts from Saalt called Hanky Panky. They have great coverage while also still managing to be cute. Most, if not all, period panties are eligible to be purchased with your HSA or FSA! — Sarah Aswell

One of my favorite discoveries of 2025 was shower tablets — also known as shower steamers. You throw them onto the floor of the shower and, over the course of your rinse, they evaporate and let off fumes infused with essential oils. Certain types can help clear out your sinuses (peppermint) or relax you for bed (lavender). They’re fun and they have a purpose. I like these from Caring Mill, which is a brand specifically for people buying HSA and FSA items. — Sarah Aswell

Neutrogena Pink Grapefruit Cleansing Wipes

These cleansing wipes are great for everything from removing grit and makeup at night to keeping in your purse for a little refresh during the day. And they smell divine! — Sarah Aswell

I’ve had my Lettuce Grow for over a year now, and it’s one of my most favorite things in our house! It’s like having your own personal salad bar. I’ve been putting pimple patches in my daughters’ holiday stockings for a few years now, but only recently have I tried them out and discovered that they actually work and are really awesome! Many of them qualify for HSA/FSA purchases, especially if they are medicated. I love these spot patches from Curology, which contain the active ingredient hydrocolloid. — Sarah Aswell

I was surprised to find that some hydration drink mixes are FSA- and HSA-approved. Which is great because sometimes when I’m feeling rundown, I just put one of these in a big glass of water and feel so much better. — Sarah Aswell

#8036. Who’s a Scaredy Cat? Keeping Cats Safe This Halloween

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Halloween can be an exciting night for families, but all that activity can leave cats feeling unsettled. Strange costumes, unfamiliar visitors, and a doorbell that rings non-stop can be overwhelming, even for cats that usually enjoy meeting new people.

The biggest concern is that a frightened cat may try to escape, while decorations, candy, and other seasonal hazards can create additional risks. A few simple changes around the home can help keep cats safe while everyone else enjoys the festivities.

Even households that don't celebrate Halloween can be affected by the extra noise and activity around the neighborhood. Excited children, unfamiliar costumes, barking dogs, loud music, and parties can create an unusually stressful environment for cats.

A frightened cat may bolt when strangers approach the house, and there's no guarantee it will head somewhere safe. A cat that escapes could become lost or run into traffic while trying to get away.

Keeping cats indoors is therefore one of the most important Halloween precautions. Even cats that normally spend time outside should remain indoors, with windows and doors securely closed.

With trick-or-treaters arriving throughout the evening, the front door may open far more often than usual. Every time it does, there's another opportunity for a cat to slip outside unnoticed.

Keeping a cat in a separate room when visitors arrive can reduce the risk, particularly if several people are coming and going. Making sure your cat is microchipped and that the registration details are up to date also improves the chances of being reunited if they do escape.

The simplest approach is to keep your cat away from the entrance for the entire evening rather than relying on everyone to remember to watch out for it.

Halloween decorations can look appealing to curious cats, but anything within reach may become a potential plaything. Curious cats can chew decorations or swallow small pieces, so it's best to avoid edible decorations and keep other items out of reach.

Carved pumpkins lit with real candles need particular care. A cat could knock one over, risking burns or even starting a fire.

Battery-operated candles offer a safer alternative. Another option is to place pumpkins outside or in a window where the cat can't reach them.

It can be tempting to dress a cat up for Halloween, especially when everyone else in the household is wearing a costume. However, many cats find clothing uncomfortable or frightening, and restrictive outfits can cause unnecessary stress.

Some cats need to wear garments for medical reasons, such as a surgical vest to protect stitches after an operation. Halloween costumes are different because they generally serve no practical purpose for the cat.

Pay attention to how a cat responds to clothing and accessories. If they seem uncomfortable or distressed, leave the costume off. There are plenty of ways to include a cat in the celebration without dressing them up.

Candy presents several potential hazards for cats. Chocolate and certain other sweets contain ingredients that can be toxic to pets, while wrappers can become choking hazards if swallowed. Even sweets that aren't directly poisonous aren't suitable cat treats, and excess sugar can contribute to health problems.

Crinkly plastic wrappers can be particularly tempting because they appeal to a cat's instinct to chase and play with small objects. Itâs all fun and games when a cat bats them around, but they could end up swallowing them.

Keep Halloween treats in a closed container somewhere the cat can't access, and make sure children understand that sharing their candy with pets isn't safe. If a cat manages to eat candy, contact a vet promptly for advice.

Cats often cope with stress by hiding somewhere they feel safe. Providing a quiet room away from visitors and noise gives them the chance to retreat until the activity dies down.

A bedroom can work well, provided it has fresh water, a litter tray, and a favorite blanket or other familiar bedding. Guests should know that the room is off-limits so the cat isn't disturbed while resting.

Giving a cat this private space can be especially helpful during parties or evenings when the front door is opening repeatedly.

It's sensible to check on a cat throughout Halloween, particularly when the household is busy. These checks help confirm that the cat is comfortable and hasn't slipped out unnoticed.

However, checking in doesn't mean coaxing a frightened cat out of its hiding place. If they have chosen a quiet spot and appear settled, let them stay there.

The aim is to make sure the cat is safe without adding more attention or activity when it would rather be left alone.

Keeping a cat safe doesn't mean they have to be excluded from the evening entirely. Cats that dislike costumes can still feature in a Halloween photoshoot without wearing anything themselves. After all, theyâre already wearing the best outfit! Dressing as a character known for having a feline companion is another way to include a cat without making them uncomfortable.

A scary movie marathon can also be a relaxed way to spend the evening together. A soft, Halloween-themed blanket and a favorite treat might encourage a cat to settle on a lap, provided it enjoys that kind of attention.

Cat-friendly treats can be offered while the humans enjoy their own candy, and cats that like catnip may appreciate a Halloween-themed toy with a little dried catnip.

Halloween should be enjoyable for the whole household, but cats don't understand why the neighborhood suddenly becomes noisier or why strangers keep appearing at the door. Keeping them indoors, removing potential hazards, and providing somewhere quiet to retreat can make the night safer and more comfortable for everyone.

#8035. Annoying Habits That Are Actually Cries for Help

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Dogs are easy to love but, on occasion, are also surprisingly difficult to live with. Barking for no reason. The leash pulling that turns a simple walk into a tug-of-war. Turning the most expensive thing in the room into a chew toyâ¦

Most dog owners have dealt with at least one of these behaviors, and itâs tempting to see them simply as bad habits. But the truth is, there is often a reason behind these irritating habits. Dogs communicate through behavior, and what looks like a nuisance is sometimes a symptom of an unmet need. The trouble is that we often get distracted by tackling that symptom when we really need to dig deeper.

Understanding what is driving an annoying or unwanted behavior can make it much easier to address.

Dogs bark for many reasons, including boredom, anxiety, fear, a perceived threat, or a desire for attention. Any dog can develop a barking habit, regardless of size.

The key is identifying what triggers it. Boredom-related barking may improve with more exercise and mental stimulation, while anxiety or fear-based barking generally requires a more structured approach. Teaching a reliable "quiet" command and avoiding accidentally rewarding attention-seeking barking can also help.

Chewing is normal for dogs, particularly teething puppies, but it becomes a problem when furniture, clothing, carpets, or walls become the preferred targets.

Boredom and anxiety can contribute to destructive chewing, as can a lack of appropriate outlets. Keeping suitable chew toys available, putting valuable items out of reach, and managing the environment while the dog learns what is acceptable can help redirect the habit.

A dog that greets visitors by launching itself at them has usually learned that jumping gets a response. Even pushing the dog away or telling it to stop can give them the attention theyâre seeking.

Ignoring the jumping and rewarding calm, four-paws-on-the-floor behavior teaches the dog that staying down gets the better response. Giving the dog an alternative behavior, such as sitting, can make the lesson clearer.

When faced with a friendly jumping dog, try the following:

Keep your arms crossed, mouth closed, and eyes averted.

Turn your back, and walk away if they keep jumping.

Ignore them until they are calm and ready to listen to your command.

Dogs beg because it has worked before. Even one successful attempt at getting food from the table can establish the habit, making it particularly difficult to break.

Feeding the dog before your mealtimes can reduce the motivation to beg, while teaching it to settle in a designated spot gives it something else to do. The biggest challenge is consistency. Giving in occasionally can keep the behavior going.

Table scraps can also pose health risks because some common human foods are harmful to dogs, while regular extras can contribute to obesity.

Leash pulling can make an otherwise enjoyable walk exhausting. Dogs often pull because they are excited and have not learned that pulling does not make the walk happen faster.

Loose-leash training takes patience. Stopping whenever the leash becomes tight and continuing only when it becomes slack teaches the dog what behavior allows the walk to continue. Rewarding the dog for walking beside the handler can reinforce the lesson, while a well-fitted harness may provide additional control during training.

Different dogs need different equipment, and what works for a small dog is not necessarily going to be suitable for a large one. Talk to your vet about the safest and most effective option for you and your dog.

Poor recall is frustrating, but it can also be dangerous if your dog runs towards traffic or another dog.

Training should start in areas with few distractions before gradually becoming more challenging. High-value rewards can make coming back more appealing, while using the recall command for unpleasant situations can create a negative association that undermines the training.

Digging is instinctive for many dogs and can also be linked to boredom or excess energy. Trying to eliminate the behavior completely may not be the most practical approach; redirection has a much higher chance of success.

Create a designated digging area, such as a sandbox or corner of the yard, making sure there is a clear distinction between this and the rest of the garden. It may be unsightly, but laying down some temporary netting or a similar obstacle in the rest of the yard can help teach your dog where they can and cannot dig. Burying toys or treats there can make the spot more appealing, while increasing daily activity may reduce the urge to dig elsewhere.

Some dogs struggle when left alone. The resulting distress can include destructive behavior, excessive barking, and other difficult behaviors.

Gradually getting a dog used to being alone, starting with very short absences and slowly increasing them, is an evidence-based approach. Providing a comfortable, safe space can also help.

Avoid making a fuss of your dog when leaving the house or on your return â your comings and goings should become part of an ordinary day, not an event. More severe cases of separation anxiety may require veterinary input or help from a behaviorist.

Aggression can have many possible causes, including fear, poor socialization, pain, territorial behavior, or negative past experiences. Because the appropriate response depends on the cause, this is one behavior where professional help is particularly important.

A veterinary examination can help rule out an underlying medical problem, including pain. A qualified trainer or behaviorist can then help address the behavior using approaches such as positive reinforcement, desensitization, and counterconditioning. Punishment can make aggression worse rather than better.

Occasional accidents can happen, but frequent or sudden indoor elimination deserves attention.

For dogs that are still learning, regular bathroom breaks and immediate positive reinforcement for going outside provide the foundation for housetraining. Enzymatic cleaners are useful for removing waste odors that can otherwise encourage a dog to return to the same spot.

If a previously house-trained dog suddenly begins having accidents, a check-up at the vet is appropriate to check for a possible medical cause.

Barking, chewing, jumping, digging, and the other behaviors on this list may be frustrating, but they rarely happen without a reason. Looking at what a dog is trying to communicate can reveal whether it needs more activity, clearer training, or a different kind of attention.

Addressing the underlying issue rather than simply trying to stop the behavior can make the problem easier to manage and help strengthen the relationship between you and your dog.

#8034. Eight Sleep’s Alexandra Zatarain on women-centered tech, the science of better sleep, and planning a career around motherhood

By Sara Goldstein Updated Nov. 12, 2026

This article is sponsored by Eight Sleep. Thank you for supporting the brands that support Motherly and mamas.

Alexandra Zatarain helped build Eight Sleep into a tech unicorn, and she’s expecting her first child in January. Going through pregnancy while running a global company has reshaped how she sees her own body, her industry and the product she’s building. On this episode of The Motherly Podcast, the co-founder of the sleep-technology company talks about the research that showed Eight Sleep’s technology was improving men’s sleep more than women’s and what the company did about it, why sleep is the most important thing women can protect, and the career advice she wishes more women heard before becoming mothers.

Meet the expert: Alexandra Zatarain is the co-founder and VP of brand and marketing at Eight Sleep, the sleep-technology company behind the Pod. The Pod is an intelligent mattress cover that cools or heats each side to your ideal temperature automatically, maximizing deep sleep and minimizing wake-ups. A marketer and brand builder, she grew Eight Sleep from launch into a tech unicorn and helped create what the company calls the sleep fitness movement. Eight Sleep now sells in 37 countries. She’s expecting her first child in January with her husband, Matteo, the company’s co-founder and CEO.

Alexandra Zatarain: So many things. I just turned 37, and I’ve seen so many friends go through pregnancy before me. After my first trimester, I felt so bad, thinking, what a terrible friend I was. When you haven’t experienced it, you have such little empathy for what a woman’s body is going through, especially when life keeps demanding so much of you and it doesn’t stop. I really didn’t understand that you could feel so different in your body for so long. It’s built so much more admiration for women and what we go through, and it’s let me embrace a feminine side of myself that in tech you usually don’t get to bring out.

Alexandra Zatarain: It’s made me realize that the only way the world out there is going to change for our benefit as women and mothers is if more of us are the ones making the decisions. I just don’t see any way around it. We have a lot of parents at Eight Sleep, every executive on our team is a parent, but as a woman the experience is completely different. Unless we can share that first-hand knowledge, it’s going to be hard to make progress as fast as we need to. It’s unfortunate that it takes the first-person experience to become that advocate, because everyone should appreciate what mothers go through, given that we all come from a mother.

Alexandra Zatarain: A couple of years ago, our clinical team, which is more than 90% women, was analyzing data from our user base and noticed our technology had been improving men’s sleep more than women’s. They asked, what are we missing in how we design this? It turned out the algorithms that manage temperature while you sleep had been fed more data representing men than women. That’s a classic problem in science, where women are underrepresented because our bodies are more complex. You have to account for where someone is in their hormonal journey, pregnancy, postpartum, perimenopause. So we invested a couple million dollars into research and developed features from it. That changed how we think about ourselves, less about helping everyone in a broad way and more about solving specific problems women have had for ages.

Alexandra Zatarain: Sleep is the most important pillar of health. You would die sooner from sleep deprivation than from food deprivation, which tells you how fundamental it is. For women it matters even more because our hormones rule our lives, and sleep is the one tool we have to regulate them. If you sleep well, your chances of better hormonal balance go up significantly. It’s the best medicine we have, more than working out, more than any meal. The challenge is that those same hormones are often playing against us, making it harder to sleep well in different seasons of life, so keeping our routines as stable as possible helps counter what our bodies are going through.

Alexandra Zatarain: The mindset piece is really important. There’s so much going on, the anxiety, the intrusive thoughts, so not being too hard on yourself is the first step. Understanding that the season will pass should put you a little more at ease, because it’s not going to be your life forever. The other piece is setting yourself up with the right systems, and the most important one is available to everyone for free, which is routine. It helps your body a lot. When you do need to sleep, it’ll be easier for your body to fall asleep because it’s used to the schedule.

Alexandra Zatarain: I’m very rigid about my sleep schedule. I travel a lot, so sleep is number one for me. I make space for eight to nine hours every night, and I’m pretty good at hitting it. I go to bed by 9:30 or 10 every single night no matter where I am in the world, and I don’t really use an alarm unless I have to wake up before 6, because my body just wakes up on its own. That schedule is the thing that’s changed my life the most. Second to that is the environment, the temperature in my room and my bed, the lights going dark, no noise.

Alexandra Zatarain: I think of myself as an athlete, and we’re all sort of athletes in a way. My sport is making decisions about how to build this business, and that means I have to train, stay healthy and think long term. It’s not a sprint. We’ve been doing this for 12 years, so the question is how do I not burn out and stay here 20 or 30 years more. I’m also lucky I built this with my husband, so there’s no real line between business and personal life for us. It’s all mixed in, but it’s so purpose-driven that achieving that purpose every day is what feeds the energy.

Alexandra Zatarain: I’m very open with them about how intentional I was. I did my embryo freezing in my early 30s because of where I was in life. And I tell them that if they want a career after they have a family, the best time to build equity in that career is to push as hard as you can before. Know what you want, because time isn’t always on our side as women. Move up the ranks, so that by the time you have kids you have more flexibility and maybe a higher income. It is possible, but it takes planning, it will require compromises, and very importantly it will require the right partner.

Alexandra Zatarain: It starts with the people around you understanding what you truly need. Sometimes it’s as simple as the encouragement of, yes, go take a nap, yes, your body’s going through a lot. It gets harder once the baby’s home and the mom is maybe exclusively breastfeeding, because it really all falls on you. So have a plan in place ahead of time for how the load is going to be shared. Our partners are much more involved than previous generations, so have those conversations early. It doesn’t end with the birth plan. That’s where everything starts.

Alexandra Zatarain: The first trimester was difficult, a lot of nausea, and it was very hard to function at the level I’m used to. I almost never get sick, so feeling sick every day was a huge shift. It put me in the trajectory to build the team that would make it possible for me to become a mother, to figure out what to delegate and who to elevate, and I’ve built a stronger team as a result. But the biggest thing is that it’s taught me to let go. I can’t control how I feel every day. As a Type A person I always want to be in control, and this has been like therapy, learning that I’m not in control of my body. I’m building a human, and it’s fine if for this season things just work differently.

#8033. Menopause Is Hurting Women at Work. Something Has To Change.

Brain fog, hot flashes, no sleep... and zero workplace support. Here’s what women can actually do about it.

I distinctly remember sitting in AP English class as a junior in high school with such horrible period cramps that it must've shown on my face. I kept staring at the clock, and eventually, my very strict, no-nonsense teacher came to my desk and asked if I was OK.

It was the first time in my life that I hadn’t felt well and advocated for myself, albeit only after being nudged.

Then, in my 20s, I was severely nauseous with my first pregnancy but kept suffering through it at work because I wanted to save up my PTO for maternity leave. Now, I work from home, but as I’m hitting my late 30s, I wonder if I’d be any better at advocating for my needs in the workplace if I had perimenopause symptoms.

Truthfully, I’m not sure I would be — and I’m far from the only one. In a new study, Womea surveyed more than 830 employed U.S. women ages 45 and older about how perimenopause or menopause symptoms affect their experiences at work.

Of those surveyed, 60% said no one at work knew they were experiencing symptoms. Meanwhile, 90% said their employers have no menopause or midlife health policies in place. An alarming 87% said their symptoms affected their job performance in the past year, and 17% believed their symptoms cost them a promotion, raise, or high-visibility project.

So what’s a woman to do when she finds her perimenopause or menopause symptoms interfering with her career? And what can we reasonably expect our employers to do about it?

Perimenopause is the hormonal transition that leads us on the lovely path to menopause. It can begin in a woman’s 30s, although it more commonly starts in her 40s. “Fun” symptoms include brain fog, sleep disruption, mood changes, hot flashes, and irregular periods.

Dr. Gillian Goddard, a board-certified endocrinologist and author of The Hormone Loop, says disrupted sleep can leave a woman feeling physically and mentally sluggish. Declining estrogen levels also affect dopamine activity, making it harder to concentrate. Research also suggests that learning new information can become more difficult during this period.

That helps explain why half of the women in the Womea survey reported experiencing brain fog or losing their train of thought during a meeting, client call, or presentation.

Women in this stage might not feel like themselves physically and emotionally, says Lauren Tetenbaum, LCSW, JD, PMH-C, MSCP, a New York-based women’s reproductive mental health expert and the author of Millennial Menopause: Preparing for Perimenopause, Menopause, and Life’s Next Period.

As a psychotherapist, Tetenbaum says many of her clients are ambitious and dedicated to their careers, but are “caught off guard by the symptoms… they were never warned about.” Not even by their own healthcare providers!

Rather than recognizing that they may need medical care or additional rest, some women catastrophize what they’re going through, she says, worrying that brain fog could be a sign of early dementia or that they’re no longer capable of meeting their own high standards. “The performance is often not the issue; it’s the self-perception,” Tetenbaum says.

Still, it’s not easy for women navigating midlife at work.

Women can feel pushed out of the workforce during major life transitions, Tetenbaum says, from matrescence to perimenopause, because they're presented with a false choice: “Sacrifice your health or wellbeing or values to work here, or leave, and don’t you dare show ‘weakness’ by asking for help.”

We shouldn’t have to choose between our health and our careers... nor should we feel obligated to disclose personal medical details to our managers just to get support.

Instead, Tetenbaum encourages women to familiarize themselves with their workplace benefits, such as health insurance coverage, PTO, and possible accommodations. (Sometimes, especially in competitive fields, employees can worry that taking PTO makes them look noncommitted. But taking care of ourselves shouldn't be seen as professional weakness. After all, we can’t bring our best selves to work if we're not feeling our best.)

Tetenbaum also strongly urges women to seek medical care rather than assume they have to push through their symptoms.

Goddard says several workplace conditions can make this phase of life more difficult for women, including insufficient restrooms, unpredictable or long hours, limited opportunities for breaks, and confined workspaces. Addressing some of these conditions could make a difference.

Employers can also review their health insurance policies to make sure menopause-related care is covered, such as menopause specialists, behavioral and psychological health care, and other relevant services, adds Tetenbaum, as well as look at ways to implement flexible schedules, remote work options, temperature controls, and uniforms that don’t exacerbate symptoms.

Of course, every individual and workplace is different. So employers should never be afraid to ask employees what would help them, she says.

As for women thinking about leaving their jobs or reducing their hours because of symptoms, Tetenbaum cautions, “Try not to make long-term decisions during a moment you feel overwhelmed.”

And the best decision we can make of all? Learning to advocate for our needs... in every stage of our careers and bodies.

#8032. Chatting About Cosmetic Animal Testing, Covid Conspiracies, & Brainless Cats | Chatty Cattys, Episode 39

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

In this episode of Catsterâs Chatty Cattys podcast, hosts Nicole and Dr. Karyn jump into an unstructured, wide-ranging discussion covering quirky pet habits, feline anatomy, and the ethics of animal testing vs. clinical research. From explaining the post-poop "zoomies" to reflecting on how decades-old feline nerve studies shed light on why cats freeze in harnesses, the hosts offer a lighthearted yet insightful look into how our pets interact with the world.

Discover the fascinating science behind feline movement, including how lower-body nerve pathways allow cats to adjust their bodies instinctively without waiting for brain signals. Dr. Karyn also breaks down why putting a coat or harness on a cat disrupts this "sixth sense," causing them to initially freeze or flop over.

Additionally, the hosts explore the difference between historical animal testing and modern, mutually beneficial clinical trials. From discussing how research into feline coronavirus treatments surprisingly overlapped with human health developments to debating why testing food or drugs on animals can be unreliable (imagine if chocolate was banned because it was tested on dogs!), this episode balances fun pet owner anecdotes with fascinating veterinary science.

The Mystery of "Poop Zoomies": Nicole and Dr. Karyn talk about how cats often sprint out of the litter box after taking a poop. They discuss how this hilarious habit stems from a mix of wild instinct (running from scent markers) and sheer physical relief.

Do Cats Always Land on Their Feet?: While cats try to land on their feet using their incredible spinal flexibility, Dr. Karyn notes it isn't an absolute ruleâpointing out that her own cat, Clutch, occasionally falls right on his butt.

How Feline Nerves Act Like a "Body Brain": Dr. Karyn discusses an old study on feline nerve pathways showing that cats can walk on a treadmill via spinal reflexes without upper brain input. This ultra-fast neural feedback gives cats rapid spatial awareness.

Why Cats Freeze in Harnesses: Because a cat's body relies heavily on sensory feedback from skin and nerves for orientation, placing clothes or a harness on them is like "blindfolding" their body, causing them to temporarily lose balance until they adapt.

Testing vs. Clinical Trials: The hosts differentiate between harmful animal testing and ethical clinical research. Modern veterinary trials often involve treating pet patients with naturally occurring conditions (like cancer or coronavirus), generating medical advancements that aid both humans and animals.

Interspecies Differences in Testing: The hosts touch on why testing human items on animals can be flawed, pointing out that many things safe for humans (like chocolate, grapes, or garlic) are toxic to pets, and vice versa.

As a certified cat-lover, Radim was excited to join the Catster team on the mission to help all the cat parents in the world by providing useful and helpful information. He used to live with two wonderful cats before embarking on his travels around the world. Radim currently lives in Slovakia, surrounded by nature and his neighbors' cat community.

#8031. Beyond the Kennel: Giving Long-Stay Shelter Dogs a Chance to Be Seen

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Their body starts to relax. Their nose hits the ground. They start sniffing everything, noticing people, wanting to explore. Sometimes they start playing. Sometimes they give me the biggest zoomies I've ever seen. Suddenly, I'm looking at a completely different dog.

I've watched it happen more times than I can count â the exact moment a long-stay shelter dog stops being "a shelter dog" and starts just being a dog. It usually happens somewhere in the middle of an adventure.

That moment is what inspired me to start Ariana's Doggos. Because when a dog has spent months living in a kennel, the version of them you see through the bars isn't necessarily their true self.

Dogs have always grounded me. They bring joy, companionship, and a sense of home, often asking for nothing in return. I started Arianaâs Doggos because I believe every shelter dog deserves to be seen for their potential, not just as an animal waiting behind bars. I know that every dog sitting in a kennel could be a companion, adventure buddy, couch potato, comedian, walking partner, and family member. They just haven't met their person yet.

I started Ariana's Doggos because I wanted to give long-stay shelter dogs the opportunity to simply be dogs outside the shelter environment, while capturing those experiences for potential adopters see them too. I don't just want to show people a dog's face and tell them that they're sweet. I want to show them what that dog could actually look like in their life.

What does this dog look like walking through a park? Do they love sniffing trails? Do they want to chase a toy around a pet store? Are they goofy? Are they cuddly? Do they want to say hello to every person they meet?

Those are the moments that can help someone imagine, "I could see this dog living with me."

Before Ariana's Doggos, I worked in fundraising, media, and storytelling. I spent three years working for a fundraising app, seeing firsthand how vital community support can be. I've always been drawn to production and storytelling, and previously worked as a radio producer. Eventually, I realized that audio alone wasn't filling my creative cup. I wanted to create something deeply visual and emotionally impactful.

At the same time, I became increasingly interested in rescue dogs and saw firsthand how the stress of a long shelter stay can affect them. I knew some rescues already gave dogs opportunities to leave the facility for walks or special outings, but I kept thinking about what could happen if those experiences became continuous storiesâthe difference between someone scrolling past a static photo and stopping to think, "Maybe that's my dog."

Ariana's Doggos started as a personal media passion project about two years ago, based in Calgary, Alberta. This year, I've begun turning it into a more structured community initiative involving shelters, local businesses, sponsors, and people who simply want to see these dogs get a little more attention.

Something important to understand about shelter dogs is that a kennel is an extremely specific, highly stressful environment. A dog may be overwhelmed, overstimulated, shut down, or frustrated by everything happening around them. Rightfully so â they don't understand why they're there.

Shelter staff and volunteers who care for these animals daily see glimpses of their true nature, but an adopter on the other side of the kennel door rarely sees beyond the first impression.

A dog sitting quietly in a corner or barking like mad can be easy to overlook. That same dog walking beside you through a park, stopping to sniff a tree, looking up at you with a goofy expression, or happily carrying around a new toy tells an entirely different story.

And sometimes that story is what gets them noticed.

As rewarding as the outings are, there is also a side of this work that breaks my heart.

The first time you take a dog out, they can be absolutely ecstatic. Everything is new. They're sniffing, exploring, and soaking everything in.

But when a dog has been waiting for a home for a long time, that excitement can start to change. They seem to understand the routine now. We're going somewhere, we're going to have fun, and eventually, we're going back to the kennel.

That's also why I believe so strongly in the importance of foster homes and other individualized resources for long-stay dogs. Foster homes are an amazing temporary solution for many dogs, but foster networks are always limited, and more dogs will always be waiting for the right foster environment or a spot to open up.

Not every dog has an immediate foster match; some need a very specific environment, routine, or space. When those resources aren't available, dogs can remain in shelters for months. And the longer they wait, the easier it can be for people to overlook them. That's exactly why I keep showing up with a camera and a leash â every video is one more chance for the right person to finally notice them.

Right now, my focus is simple: one dog at a time. Taking shelter dogs out, creating meaningful experiences and exposure for them, and turning those adventures into story-driven videos that reach people far beyond the shelter walls.

With Ariana's Doggos, the outing doesn't end when the dog goes back. The digital story keeps working long after the day is over, putting dogs in front of potential adopters.

I also have a bigger, long-term dream. Eventually, I would love to build a dedicated, foster-scale facility that could work alongside existing shelters and foster networks.

It wouldn't replace shelters or traditional foster homes. Instead, I envision it as a centralized resource for shelter dogs who need extra exposure to find a home, basic training to help them fit into the right home, or a more individualized setting for dogs struggling with the shelter environment.

Most importantly, I want that environment to combine professional care with maximum public visibility through media and storytelling, preparing them fully for their future families.

I don't know exactly what Ariana's Doggos will look like years from now. Right now, I'm still building the foundation through these individual adventures and learning what works.

Every time I take a dog out, I'm reminded that these animals are so much more than their shelter profile.

They're goofy,  complicated, affectionate. They're curious and occasionally chaotic. They're individuals. They can become such an important part of someone's life, and they deserve to be seen that way.

I may not be able to find a home for every shelter dog, but I can give them a day where they aren't a shelter dog. They're just a dog.

Sniffing a trail, choosing a toy, meeting a stranger, or getting the zoomies. A dog discovering something new.

And I can take those moments and put them in front of potential adopters who may never have looked twice at them in a kennel.

Because sometimes finding a dog a home starts with being seen.

You don't have to adopt to make a difference. Just by sharing these videos, you help potential adopters find their new best friend. Whether you can donate to support these adventures or simply follow along on Facebook, Instagram, and YouTube, every bit helps. Local businesses and organizations can also get involved by sponsoring an adventure, hosting a shelter dog for an outing, or exploring other collaborations. Iâd love to hear from you.

The ultimate goal is to build a vibrant community around these dogs â to get more people seeing them, talking about them, commenting, and giving them the chance to be seen for who they really are.

Every shelter dog has a story. They just need someone to tell it.

This time of year may see reduced raised bed activity, but these quick tasks can prep your beds for the cold months ahead and ensure better productivity when spring returns

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Raised beds are cosy homes for vegetables, annuals and perennials, but, like all homes, they require maintenance. When you prepare raised beds for winter, you make things easier for all your plants next season. With proper care, you can ensure that your raised bed frames and soils are safe from frost and winter rain, and that any plants you subsequently add can hit the ground running.

Because raised beds sit above the ground, their soil cools down faster, is more exposed to biting winter wind, and faces heavier nutrient leaching from seasonal downpours. Neglected beds may develop drainage issues or lose valuable nutrients. The best raised garden bed ideas protect your soil from winter’s worst. Taking a few simple winter-smart steps now can help to extend the life of the soil, prevent nutrient leaching, and make a strong spring harvest far more likely.

Best of all, these winterizing tasks are quick, low-effort wins. Whether you are tending a single cedar herb box or galvanized steel troughs, prepping your beds now guarantees more fertile soil in spring, earlier planting windows, healthier perennials, and your most bountiful harvests yet. Here’s how to protect your raised beds through winter.

Before you start these tasks, take a quick inventory of your raised bed setup. Size, depth, and construction material can all influence how your beds weather the cold. Wooden beds (like cedar, redwood, or pine) offer natural insulation, but absorb moisture, making them prone to swelling, warping, or fungal rot if soggy debris sits against the boards all winter. You can buy a wood sealant to protect bed frames from winter moisture, as long as it is safe, such as Seal It Green’s Plant-Based Garden Bed Sealer, available from Amazon.

Galvanized metal beds and stone beds are virtually rot-proof, but they conduct cold rapidly. This can mean that soil near the outer walls might freeze and thaw faster, putting perimeter plant roots under extra stress. Shallow beds under 10 inches (25cm) deep can also freeze solid much sooner than deep 18-24-inch (45-60cm) troughs. Bear all this in mind when tackling the jobs here.

Where you live has a part to play, too. In northern regions (USDA hardiness zones 3-6), you need to complete winter prep before the top few inches of soil freeze solid, typically by late November. In milder southern and coastal areas (zones 7-10), winterizing is more about suppressing cool-season weeds, preventing heavy rain from washing away nutrients, and tucking in cold-hardy crops like garlic or kale.

Visit your beds after rainfall to check soil moisture and drainage before beginning your winter tune-up. You can buy a soil temperature and moisture diagnostic tool, such as the Daybetter Soil Meter 4-in-1 from Walmart, to check whether raised bed soil is ready for cover crops or mulch. Then you are ready to get your beds in shape with these tips…

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

It used to be standard advice to strip beds bare in fall, but leaving soil naked can expose it to erosion, deplete soil nutrition, and destroy vital overwintering habitats for beneficial pollinators and predatory beetles. Instead, be selective about cleanup. Pull out all spent annual veg and frost-blackened fruiting crops such as tomatoes, peppers, and squash. Also remove persistent weeds. Don’t toss these into the compost pile, but bag them for municipal green waste.

For healthy, disease-free annuals like beans, peas, or marigolds, snip stems at soil level with clean pruners such as the Felco F2 Bypass Pruning Shears, available from Amazon. Leaving the roots in the ground prevents soil disturbance and feeds earthworms and soil microbes as they decompose over winter. Finally, remove bamboo stakes, tomato cages, and trellises, scrubbing off clinging soil and fungal spores with a mild diluted bleach or vinegar wash before storing them dry.

Intensive raised bed gardening draws heavily on soil reserves over summer, leaving it depleted by November. Replenishing fertility now allows rain, snow, and microbial activity to work on amendments before spring planting begins. Gently loosen any compacted soil using a broadfork or standard garden fork. Push the tines in and rock back slightly. If you need a good fork, the Ames 4-Tine Forged Spading Fork from The Home Depot can help improve drainage without churning up soil structure.

Spread a generous 2-3-inch (5-8cm) layer of aged organic compost, leaf mold, or well-rotted manure across the surface. Avoid hot, uncomposted manure, which can burn roots and leach excess nitrates. If your soil test indicates low phosphorus or acidity (common in high-rainfall regions) then add slow-acting mineral amendments such as rock phosphate, greensand, or garden lime. These require several months to break down and adjust soil chemistry before spring crops go in.

Once your soil is fed, your next mission is to protect the surface from winter erosion, temperature swings, and nutrient washout. Your first option is to tuck the soil under a thick blanket of fluffy organic mulch. For beds lying fallow, or housing perennial herbs and cold-hardy greens, apply a 3-4-inch (8-10cm) layer of shredded fall leaves, clean weed-free straw, or pine needles over your compost layer. Avoid heavy mats of wet grass clippings or unshredded oak leaves, which block oxygen and harbor slugs.

Alternatively, in mild regions, you can sow fast-establishing cover crops like winter rye, crimson clover, hairy vetch, or tillage daikon radish. Their roots help to anchor soil against torrential rain. They also scavenge leftover nitrogen and break up deep compaction, ready to be chopped down and turned 3-4 weeks before spring planting. Buy Outside Pride Crimson Clover Seeds from Amazon for just a few dollars.

Shallow-rooted perennials and newly planted spring bulbs in raised beds face a couple of threats: frost heaving and hungry digging pests. Repeated freezing nights and thawing sunny days can cause wet soil to expand and contract, pushing shallow crowns such as coral bells, foamflowers, and strawberries out of the earth. To prevent frost heave, wait until the ground has frozen lightly. Then mound 3-4 inches (8-10cm) of shredded leaves or evergreen boughs around the crowns. This locks in consistent cold temperatures rather than trapping warmth that delays dormancy.

Raised beds packed with newly planted tulips, crocus, or ranunculus bulbs are very tempting for squirrels, voles, and chipmunks. Lay half-inch hardware cloth or chicken wire flat across the soil surface, weighing down the edges with bricks or landscape staples. If you need a good mesh then Ashman Online Hardware Cloth, available from The Home Depot, can stop squirrels and voles from digging up bulbs. Remove it in early spring as green shoots emerge.

Winter can put structural stress on raised beds, making this the ideal time for a quick inspection. Walk the perimeter and check corner brackets, screws, and timber boards for splitting, wood rot, or rust. Tighten any loose hardware and brace any bowing sides, especially on long wooden beds over 8 feet (2.4m) long. Place a spirit level across the top edges to ensure frames haven't settled unevenly. You can buy Allfun Metal Raised Bed Brackets from Amazon to reinforce ageing or bowing wooden bed corners.

Inspect drainage after heavy rain. Note whether the water pools, where it pools, and how rapidly it clears up. Well-draining soil should clear water within 15-20 minutes. If puddles linger, check whether landscape fabric or cardboard at the base has clogged with silt, and use a garden fork to punch deep drainage channels into the subsoil. Finally, check soil height. Ideally, the soil needs to sit 1-2 inches (2.5-5cm) below the top rim. Top up sunken beds with a 50/50 blend of topsoil and compost.

If your raised beds house overwintering crops or borderline-hardy perennials, adding some protection can extend harvests and save tender specimens from icy blasts. Because raised beds warm up faster than surrounding ground, they respond well to low tunnels and protective covers. For grafted roses in deep raised beds, mound 6-10 inches (15-25cm) of compost, aged bark, straw or soil over the graft union.

For tender perennials, drape medium-weight breathable horticultural fleece (frost cloth) over flexible PVC or wire hoops anchored into the inside edges of the bed frame. For a breathable winter frost blanket, you can buy AGFabric Floating Row Covers from Walmart to shield overwintering veg and tender perennials, while allowing light and moisture through. Secure edges with spring clamps so that winter gales don’t whip covers away. Another good option is a straw-filled wire cage.

Need more ideas for getting the most from your plants, indoors and out, and looking for the best seasonal expert advice delivered straight to your inbox? Sign up for the free Gardening Know How Newsletter!

Teo Spengler is a master gardener and a docent at the San Francisco Botanical Garden, where she hosts public tours. She has studied horticulture and written about nature, trees, plants and gardening for more than two decades. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Her extended family includes some 30 houseplants and hundreds of outdoor plants, including 250 trees, which are her main passion. Spengler currently splits her life between San Francisco and the French Basque Country, though she was raised in Alaska, giving her experience of gardening in a range of climates.

#8029. 35 Desert Baby Names For Your New Little Adventure Buddy

From A to Z (or in this case, Alan to Zenith).

If you’re a parent who lives to visit the next national park on their must-see list — the kind everyone turns to when they need to borrow camping supplies, who has probably seriously considered #vanlife at least once — of course you’re leaning toward nature-inspired baby names for your new little one. Whether you live in an arid region or they’re your favorite places to visit, these desert baby names will remind you of golden sands and endless blue skies.

Mojave asters are perennial flowering shrubs covered in beautiful purple blooms. This is a beautiful name choice if you like the idea of an earthy girl name, but floral names often strike you as too feminine. It gets bonus points for also meaning “star” in Greek.

A canyon is a deep, narrow valley with steep, rocky sides, and usually there is a river at the bottom that has carved all that rock away over time. It would make a strong boy’s name, and subtly remind him to persevere, like water against stone.

Joshua Tree National Park connects the Mojave and Colorado deserts, and is known for its iconic bristled trees. While many desert baby names feel a little woo woo and whimsical, Joshua is a classic that’ll fly under the radar when you need it to.

This name means “fire”, if you’re drawing from the Arabic roots, or “my light” if you’re referencing the Turkish version. Something about it gives cool girl, yet grounded, and all of its meanings tie back to the heat and brightness of the desert.

Do any of these names sound just right for your the new baby in your nature-loving family?

#8028. Your kid needs you to have hobbies outside of motherhood. Here’s why

Hobbies aren’t a luxury for moms. They boost well-being, nurture identity, and show our children what a full life looks like.

By Lauren Ramakrishna Updated Nov. 13, 2026

Twenty-four years. That’s how long it had been since I last stood atop a swim block, preparing to dive in for a timed race in an official meet.

A whistle blew. The crowd hushed to silence. A monotone call came over the loudspeaker, “Swimmers, take your mark,” followed by a loud electronic beep that signaled the start of the race. I felt the cold rush of water overtake my body upon diving in. The neurons in my brain feverishly told my muscles to complete the strokes I’d learned decades before. In seconds, it was done. I finished the race.

When I got out of the pool, I walked over to my kids. My son, a competitive swimmer himself, looked at me and earnestly said, “Wow, Mom. I’m proud of you.”

Like most moms, I have a packed schedule. I work, parent, volunteer at school, shepherd my two kids to practices and social gatherings, throw meals together, walk the dog, and occasionally find a moment to breathe. But over the past couple of years, I watched my growing kids, now ages 12 and 9, discover and engage in passions that light them up. It left me wondering, why not me, too?

“A recurring theme in my practice is women feeling they’ve lost their individual identities somewhere between work, parenting, and meeting everyone else’s needs,” says Carly Snyder, a New York City–based reproductive and perinatal psychiatrist. “Part of my work involves helping women recognize that their own interests and needs are legitimate.”

In an effort to start prioritizing my own interests, I jumped at the chance to sign up for a summer swim league for adults aptly named “Grown-Up Swimming.” The whole experience reignited my love for swimming, and it showed me and my kids that I’m more than just a mom.

Research highlights a multitude of benefits earned by pursuing hobbies. Hobbyists often have wider social networks, improved mental health markers, and enhanced positive emotions.

Hobbies offer a particularly important lifeline for mothers, who often report losing themselves to the demanding needs of family life. That rings true for Kaitlyn Edington, an art educator and mom of two who recalls struggling after returning to work as a teacher following the birth of her first child. “I was so depleted,” Edington says. She spent her workdays teaching with short breaks to pump, often bringing her computer into her pumping room so she could catch up on work, then went home to full nights of infant care.

One day while scrolling on Instagram, Edington saw an artist posting images of her sketchbook paintings. “She changed my life,” Edington says. “Her sketchbook paintings were so loose and free, and she was encouraging people to draw everyday. I remember thinking, ‘If I have to pump two to three times a day, which I absolutely hate, why not pair it with something that I love?’” From then on, Edington sketched when she pumped, and ultimately developed a habit of daily sketching that she continues 10 years later.

No longer in the pumping phase of life, Edington ensures she gets time to sketch by waking up before her kids. “I hold the habit of waking up before my kids as sacred,” she says. “I need that time, when nobody needs me. It’s my emotional rest.”

Science backs Edington’s belief that her hobby stabilizes her mental health. “Reengaging in meaningful, enjoyable activities can be therapeutically valuable,” Snyder says. “Behavioral activation, an evidence-based treatment for depression, specifically emphasizes reconnecting with activities that provide pleasure, purpose, or a sense of accomplishment.”

Snyder has three children, ages 19, 16, and 11, and throughout their lives she has maintained her dedication to skiing, cycling, yoga and running, completing a total of 19 marathons. She knows her kids benefit from her hobbies. Each time Snyder trains for an upcoming marathon, “[My kids] witness my commitment, discipline, setbacks, and perseverance,” she says. “Watching a parent pursue a hobby provides opportunities to observe persistence, emotional regulation, problem-solving, and enjoyment.”

But those benefits are secondary to the impacts hobbies have on the women pursuing them. “I think we’ve become so accustomed to framing everything mothers do in terms of how it benefits their children,” Snyder says. “Women are entitled to happiness and fulfillment for their own sake.”

It’s simply an added bonus that when mom is happy for mom’s sake, the benefits for her kids naturally follow, according to multiple studies linking a mother’s well-being with her child’s. Plus, kids also learn that all stages of adulthood, including those under the umbrella of parenting, can include personal fulfillment, curiosity, and growth.

The best way to start a hobby is to let yourself reconnect with something you already love. I remembered how much joy I got out of competing in swim meets in high school, and I was eager to recreate that glee. Ask yourself, “What did I love when I was a kid or a young adult?”

Your hobby doesn’t have to involve intense commitment. “Reading, gardening, dancing, listening to music, or simply spending time alone can be just as meaningful as running a marathon,” Snyder says.

Search online for local groups involved in the activity you want to pursue. Your local library may have resources to help you get started as well.

When you’re ready to commit, set realistic goals. Start by focusing on your hobby consistently for just 10-15 minutes per day. Showing up is the main goal.

“Motherhood should expand a woman’s identity, not erase it,” Snyder advises. Which hobby will help expand yours?
